cards.q: What are top-level statements?
cards.a:
Code written directly in Program.cs outside any class, wrapped in Main for you

The compiler wraps code written outside any class in a generated `Main` method. They are not a separate step before `Main`: they are its body.

cards.q: Why is the type of Console.ReadLine() string? and not plain string?
cards.a:
It returns null when the input has ended, and `?` says the string may be null

`string?` is a string that may be null, and `ReadLine` gives null when there is no more input. An empty line is still a real string, "", not null.

cards.q: What does `Console.Write("a"); Console.WriteLine("b"); Console.Write("c");` print?
cards.a:
ab on one line, then c on the next

Write does not end the line; WriteLine does, after printing its text.

cards.q: Which type should hold an amount of money, and why?
cards.a:
decimal, because it stores decimal fractions like 0.10 exactly

`decimal` stores base-10 fractions exactly. `double` is binary, so amounts like 0.1 + 0.2 come out with rounding errors, however many digits it has.

cards.q: After int[] y = x; y[0] = 5; what is x[0]?
cards.a:
5

Arrays are reference types: `y = x` copies the reference, so x and y are the same array.

cards.q: What does `var n = 10 / 4;` give?
cards.a:
2, an int

Both operands are int, so the division is whole-number division and var infers int.

cards.q: What are 23 / 4 and 23 % 4 with ints?
cards.a:
5 and 3

Integer division drops the fraction, giving 5, and `%` is the remainder: 23 = 4 × 5 + 3. You only get 5.75 when one side is a double.

cards.q: Why is if (name != null && name.Length > 0) safe when name is null?
cards.a:
&& stops when the left side is false, so name.Length is never evaluated

`&&` short-circuits: if the left side is false, the right side never runs. Reading `name.Length` on null would throw a NullReferenceException.

cards.q: What does `Math.Round(3.5) + Math.Round(4.5)` give?
cards.a:
8

Banker's rounding takes 3.5 to 4 and 4.5 to 4, the even neighbours.

cards.q: What does $"[{x,-6}]" do?
cards.a:
Writes x left-aligned in 6 characters, padded with spaces on the right

In `{value,width}` a negative width left-aligns and a positive one right-aligns. The width is a minimum, so a longer value is not cut.

cards.q: Why use a StringBuilder in a loop instead of +=?
cards.a:
Strings are immutable, so each += copies the whole string; StringBuilder appends in place

A string never changes: `+=` builds a new string and copies everything so far, which gets slow in a loop. `StringBuilder` grows one buffer instead.

cards.q: What is `"hello"[1..^1]`?
cards.a:
"ell"

From index 1 up to, not including, the last character.

cards.q: When does a do-while loop differ from a while loop?
cards.a:
A do-while always runs its body at least once, since it checks the condition after it

The condition of a do-while is tested after the body, so the body runs once even when the condition is false from the start.

cards.q: What does continue do inside a for loop?
cards.a:
Skips the rest of this round's body, runs i++, then goes on with the next round

`continue` ends only the current round. In a for loop the update part (`i++`) still runs before the condition is checked again.

cards.q: How many times does `for (int i = 0; i < 10; i += 3)` run its body?
cards.a:
4

i takes the values 0, 3, 6 and 9.

cards.q: What is the difference between ref and out?
cards.a:
ref needs the variable assigned before the call; out needs the method to assign it

Both pass the caller's own variable, not a copy. The difference is who must assign it: the caller before a `ref` call, the method before it returns for `out`.

cards.q: Can optional parameters come before required ones?
cards.a:
No: optional parameters must come after all the required ones

Optional parameters go at the end of the list. Named arguments let callers skip some optional ones, but they do not change where they may be declared.

cards.q: Given `static int F(int x) { x = 5; return x; }`, what is `a` after `int a = 1; F(a);`?
cards.a:
1

The argument is passed by value: F changes its own copy.

cards.q: Why remove items from a list inside a loop by going backwards?
cards.a:
Removing shifts later items down; going backwards, the indexes still to visit do not move

Removing at i moves every later item down one place. Counting forwards with a for loop then silently skips an item; it does not throw (foreach is the loop that throws when the list changes).

cards.q: After var b = a; b.Add(1); does a contain the 1?
cards.a:
Yes: a and b refer to the same list

A List is a reference type, so `b = a` copies the reference, not the items. To copy the list, write `new List<int>(a)`.

cards.q: What does `new List<int> { 3, 1, 2 }.IndexOf(5)` return?
cards.a:
-1

IndexOf returns -1 when the value is not in the list.

cards.q: What happens when you read dict["missing"]?
cards.a:
It throws KeyNotFoundException; use TryGetValue or GetValueOrDefault instead

Reading a missing key with the indexer throws. Returning the default is what `GetValueOrDefault` does, and only writing `dict["missing"] = v` adds a key.

cards.q: What does HashSet.Add return for a value already in the set?
cards.a:
false, and the set is unchanged

A set never holds duplicates, so `Add` reports false and changes nothing. Throwing for a duplicate is what `Dictionary.Add` does.

cards.q: Which collection should store "has this user name been taken?" for a million names?
cards.a:
HashSet<string>

HashSet.Contains takes about the same time however many items there are; a list checks every item.

cards.q: What is the difference between First() and FirstOrDefault()?
cards.a:
First throws when nothing matches; FirstOrDefault returns the type's default

`First` throws an InvalidOperationException for no match. `FirstOrDefault` returns `default`: null for classes, 0 for int.

cards.q: When does a Where query actually run?
cards.a:
When it is enumerated (foreach, ToList, Count, Sum), and again each time

LINQ queries are deferred and not cached: every enumeration runs the query again. Call `ToList()` to run it once and keep the results.

cards.q: What does `new[] { 3, 1, 2 }.OrderBy(x => x).Select(x => x * 2).Last()` give?
cards.a:
6

Sorted 1 2 3, doubled 2 4 6, the last is 6.

cards.q: What does name?.Length ?? 0 give when name is null?
cards.a:
0

`?.` gives null instead of throwing, and `??` replaces that null with 0.

cards.q: Why does the order of switch arms matter?
cards.a:
Arms are tried from the top, and the first one that matches wins

Only the first matching arm runs, so a broad arm (like `_`) above a narrower one hides it. The compiler reports an arm that can never be reached.

cards.q: What does `x is > 10 and < 20` test?
cards.a:
x is between 10 and 20, both excluded

Relational patterns combined with and must both match.

cards.q: What is the difference between { get; init; } and { get; set; }?
cards.a:
init allows setting only while the object is created; set allows changes at any time

An `init` property can be set in the constructor or an object initializer (`new P { X = 1 }`), but not after that. `set` allows changes at any time.

cards.q: Two variables hold different Point objects with the same X and Y. What does == give for a class?
cards.a:
False: for classes == compares references, not contents

Unless the class defines its own `==`, it checks whether both variables refer to the same object. Records compare their contents instead.

cards.q: Where can a `private` field be used?
cards.a:
Only inside the class that declares it

private members are visible only inside their own class; protected adds subclasses.

cards.q: What does with do on a record?
cards.a:
Creates a copy with the listed properties changed, leaving the original as it was

`p with { X = 5 }` copies every property of p and then changes X. The original record is untouched.

cards.q: Why are mutable structs risky?
cards.a:
Assignments copy them, so code often changes a copy by mistake

A struct is a value type: assigning or returning it makes a copy, and the original stays the same. Changing every copy at once is what reference types do, which is why the bug is easy to miss.

cards.q: `record R(int A);` What is `new R(1) == new R(1)`?
cards.a:
True

Records compare by value: all properties are equal.

cards.q: What is the difference between abstract and virtual?
cards.a:
An abstract member has no body and must be overridden; a virtual one has a body that may be

`abstract` declares a member with no body that every concrete derived class must override. `virtual` gives a default body that derived classes may replace.

cards.q: Can you write new Shape("x") when Shape is abstract?
cards.a:
No: an abstract class cannot be instantiated, only derived from

An abstract class's constructor exists for derived classes to call with `base(...)`; you can only create objects of a derived, non-abstract class.

cards.q: `Shape s = new Circle(1);` `Area` is virtual and overridden in Circle. Which Area runs for `s.Area()`?
cards.a:
Circle's, because the object is a Circle

Virtual calls use the type of the actual object, not of the variable.

cards.q: How many interfaces can a class implement?
cards.a:
Any number, plus at most one base class

C# allows only one base class, but a class can implement as many interfaces as it needs, alongside that base class.

cards.q: Why does Greeter take an IClock instead of calling DateTime.Now itself?
cards.a:
So a test can give it a fixed clock, and its behaviour can be checked without editing Greeter

Depending on an interface lets the caller choose the clock: a fixed one in tests, the real one in the program. Greeter itself never changes.

cards.q: A method only loops over its argument with foreach. Which parameter type is best?
cards.a:
IEnumerable<T>

Accept the most general type that does the job, so callers can pass any collection.

cards.q: Why can a static method not use this?
cards.a:
It runs without an object, so there is no instance for this

A static method belongs to the class, not to an object, so `this` does not exist there at all (it is a compile error, not a null).
cards.lessonTitle: Static Members, Extension Methods and Namespaces

cards.q: What makes a method an extension method?
cards.a:
It is static, in a static class, and its first parameter is marked with this

The `this` before the first parameter is what lets you call `s.Shout()` as if it were the type's own method. The type itself is not changed or derived from.
cards.lessonTitle: Static Members, Extension Methods and Namespaces

cards.q: What is the difference between const and static readonly?
cards.a:
const is fixed when compiling; static readonly is set once at run time

Both are read-only. A const is baked in at compile time and limited to simple types; a static readonly field is set once when the program runs and can be any type.
cards.lessonTitle: Static Members, Extension Methods and Namespaces

cards.q: What does where T : IComparable<T> allow inside a generic method?
cards.a:
Calling CompareTo on values of type T

The constraint promises that every T has a `CompareTo` method, so `a.CompareTo(b)` compiles. Operators like `<` are not part of the interface.

cards.q: Why can a List<Circle> be passed as IEnumerable<Shape> but not as List<Shape>?
cards.a:
IEnumerable<T> only hands items out; a List<Shape> would let you add a square to the circles

`IEnumerable<out T>` is covariant because it is read-only. If a `List<Circle>` were a `List<Shape>`, `Add(new Square())` would put a square into a list of circles, so the conversion is not allowed even with a cast.

cards.q: What is `default(T)` when T is `string`?
cards.a:
null

string is a reference type, so its default is null.

cards.q: What is the type of a lambda that takes a string and returns a bool?
cards.a:
Func<string, bool>

In `Func` the last type argument is the return type; `Action` returns nothing. `Predicate<string>` also fits.

cards.q: Why invoke an event with TooHot?.Invoke(...)?
cards.a:
With no subscribers the event is null, and ?. skips the call

An event nobody has subscribed to is null. Calling it directly would throw a NullReferenceException; `?.` simply does nothing.

cards.q: What does this print? `int x = 1; Func<int> f = () => x * 10; x = 5; Console.WriteLine(f());`
cards.a:
50

The lambda captures the variable x, and reads it when called.

cards.q: Why should catch (Exception) come after catch (FormatException)?
cards.a:
Catches are tried in order, and Exception would catch everything

The first catch whose type matches handles the exception. `Exception` matches every exception, so a specific catch after it could never run, and the compiler rejects it.

cards.q: What is the difference between throw; and throw e; inside a catch?
cards.a:
throw; rethrows with the original stack trace; throw e; resets the trace to the current line

Both rethrow the same exception, but `throw e;` starts the stack trace again at the catch, hiding where the error really happened.

cards.q: When does a finally block run?
cards.a:
Always, whether or not an exception happened

`finally` runs after the try, after a catch, or while an uncaught exception passes through. It is for clean-up that must happen in every case.

cards.q: Why is the garbage collector not enough for files?
cards.a:
It frees memory at some unknown later time, but a file must be closed promptly

The collector runs when memory is needed, which may be much later. A file must be closed promptly so its data is written and other programs can open it.

cards.q: What does a using statement guarantee?
cards.a:
Dispose is called when the block is left, normally or by an exception

`using` works like try/finally around the block: `Dispose` always runs. It does not catch the exception, which still reaches the caller.

cards.q: A class has a private StreamWriter field. What should the class do?
cards.a:
Implement IDisposable and dispose the writer in its own Dispose method

An owner of a disposable resource must be disposable itself and release what it owns.

cards.q: When does the code inside an iterator method start running?
cards.a:
At the first MoveNext, when the sequence is first enumerated

Calling an iterator method only creates the iterator. Its body starts when someone asks for the first item, for example a foreach.

cards.q: Why can Fibonacci() loop forever without hanging the program?
cards.a:
It is lazy: it only computes the next value when asked, and Take(10) stops asking after ten

Each `yield return` pauses the method until the next item is requested. Once `Take(10)` has ten items it stops asking, so the loop never runs further.

cards.q: An iterator method throws ArgumentException on its first line. When is it thrown?
cards.a:
When the sequence is first enumerated

The whole body, including the first line, is deferred until enumeration begins.

cards.q: What does await do to the thread while the awaited task is not finished?
cards.a:
It frees the thread; the method resumes when the task is done

`await` returns control to the caller instead of blocking, so the thread can do other work. The rest of the method runs after the task completes.

cards.q: Why should you not call .Result on a task?
cards.a:
It blocks the thread, and on a UI thread it can deadlock

`.Result` waits by blocking, which wastes the thread. On a UI thread that can deadlock, because the task may need that very thread to finish; `await` instead.

cards.q: Two independent operations take 1 second each. How long does `await Task.WhenAll(A(), B())` take?
cards.a:
About 1 second

Both tasks are started before waiting, so they run at the same time.

cards.q: Why can count++ from several threads give a total that is too low?
cards.a:
count++ reads, adds and writes in separate steps, so two threads can read the same old value

If two threads both read 7 and both write 8, one increment is lost. `Interlocked.Increment` or a lock makes the step atomic.

cards.q: Who creates the CancellationTokenSource and who checks the token?
cards.a:
The caller creates and cancels the source; the worker receives the token and checks it

Cancellation is cooperative: nothing stops the worker unless it checks the token (or passes it to methods that do).

cards.q: Which is the right tool to run a heavy calculation without freezing a desktop app's window?
cards.a:
await Task.Run(() => Calculate())

An async method still runs its CPU work on the calling thread; Task.Run moves it to the thread pool.

cards.q: What is the difference between File.ReadAllLines and File.ReadLines?
cards.a:
ReadAllLines loads every line into an array at once; ReadLines reads lazily as you loop

`ReadLines` returns a lazy sequence, so a huge file never has to fit in memory. The whole file as one string is `ReadAllText`.

cards.q: Why use Path.Combine instead of joining strings with a backslash?
cards.a:
The separator differs between operating systems, and Path.Combine uses the right one

Windows uses `\` and Linux and macOS use `/`. `Path.Combine` picks the right separator and avoids doubled slashes; it does not touch the disk.

cards.q: A StreamWriter is created without using and never disposed. What can happen?
cards.a:
The last lines stay in its buffer and never reach the file

Writers buffer data, and disposing flushes the buffer and closes the file. Without it the end of the data can be lost and the file can stay locked.

cards.q: When can JsonSerializer.Deserialize<T> return null?
cards.a:
When the JSON text is the literal null

Invalid JSON throws a JsonException, and missing properties are just left at their defaults. Only the JSON text `null` gives null.

cards.q: How do you make the JSON use camelCase names for PascalCase properties?
cards.a:
Set PropertyNamingPolicy = JsonNamingPolicy.CamelCase in JsonSerializerOptions

The naming policy renames properties when writing (and reading). Case-insensitive only affects reading, and by default the names are written as declared. `[JsonPropertyName]` renames single properties.

cards.q: A JSON object lacks a property that the record has. What does Deserialize do by default?
cards.a:
Leaves that property at its default value (null, 0, false)

Missing properties are not an error unless you require them.

cards.q: Why should one HttpClient be reused instead of creating one per request?
cards.a:
Each new client can hold sockets open after use, and many under load can run out of them

A client can send many requests, even at once. Creating and disposing one per request leaves connections lingering, which can exhaust the machine's sockets.

cards.q: Which failures are worth retrying?
cards.a:
Transient ones: timeouts, 429 Too Many Requests and 5xx server errors

A 4xx error such as 400, 401, 403 or 404 says the request itself is wrong, so sending it again gives the same answer. Retrying everything also adds load to a failing server.

cards.q: What does `response.EnsureSuccessStatusCode()` do for a 404 response?
cards.a:
Throws an HttpRequestException

It throws for any status outside 200-299.

cards.q: Why put the domain logic in a class library instead of the console project?
cards.a:
So tests, a UI or a web API can reference and reuse it, free of input and output code

A library can be referenced by any number of projects. Keeping Console calls out of it means each front end decides how to show results.

cards.q: What does dotnet run -- report 2026-03 pass to the program?
cards.a:
The arguments after --: "report" and "2026-03" arrive in args

`--` separates dotnet's own options from the program's arguments, and args are split at spaces, so args is ["report", "2026-03"].

cards.q: Which project setting turns on warnings for possibly-null references?
cards.a:
Nullable

<Nullable>enable</Nullable> turns on nullable reference types.

cards.q: What is the difference between [Fact] and [Theory]?
cards.a:
A Fact is one test without parameters; a Theory runs once for each InlineData set

A Theory is a parameterised test: each `[InlineData(...)]` line gives one set of arguments and one test run.

cards.q: Why does an InvoiceService that takes an IClock test more easily than one that reads DateTime.Now?
cards.a:
A test can give it a fixed clock, so the due date is the same on every run

With `DateTime.Now` the expected due date changes every day. A fixed clock makes the result predictable.

cards.q: xUnit creates a new instance of the test class for each test. What does that guarantee?
cards.a:
Tests cannot affect each other through instance fields

A fresh object per test keeps tests independent. Static state is still shared, which is one more reason to avoid it.

cards.q: What is a composition root?
cards.a:
The one place near the program's start where objects are created and connected

Only the composition root knows which concrete classes are used; the rest of the code just receives its dependencies through constructors.

cards.q: Why should a singleton not depend on a scoped service?
cards.a:
The singleton lives for the whole app and would keep one scoped instance forever

A singleton is created once, so it captures the scoped instance it got first and shares it across all scopes. Being created on every request is what a transient service is.

cards.q: An environment variable `Reminders__Channel=sms` is set and appsettings.json says "email". Which value does configuration give?
cards.a:
sms

Environment variables are added after appsettings.json, so they override it; __ separates sections.

cards.q: Why must a UI event handler not run a 5-second calculation directly?
cards.a:
It runs on the UI thread, so the window freezes until it finishes

While the handler runs, the UI thread cannot draw or respond to clicks. Await the work instead (with `Task.Run` for CPU work).

cards.q: What does INotifyPropertyChanged do for data binding?
cards.a:
It raises PropertyChanged when a property changes, so bound controls read the new value

Binding reads a property once; the PropertyChanged event is how the view model tells the controls that a value has changed.

cards.q: In MVVM, where does the rule "the Add button is disabled while the title is empty" belong?
cards.a:
In the view model, as the command's CanExecute

The view model holds the screen's behaviour; the view only binds to it.

cards.q: Why is the report a pure function of the ledger and the month?
cards.a:
It can be tested with any ledger built in memory, with no side effects to set up or clean up

A pure function's result depends only on its arguments, so a test just builds a ledger and checks the report. No files or clock are involved.

cards.q: Why store a version number in the saved file?
cards.a:
So a later version of the app can recognise and convert files written by older versions

When the format changes, the version number tells the loader which layout it is reading, so old files keep working.

cards.q: In this design, where should the rule "an amount of 0 is not allowed" be checked?
cards.a:
In the domain, in Ledger.Add

Rules live in the domain so every way of adding a transaction obeys them; the command handler at the edge turns the error into a message.

cards.q: If you define `operator ==`, what else must you write?
cards.a:
`operator !=`, and overrides of `Equals` and `GetHashCode` that agree with it

C# requires `==` and `!=` to be defined in pairs. `Equals` and `GetHashCode` should give the same answers too, or collections and `==` will disagree.

cards.q: Why should an implicit conversion never throw?
cards.a:
It happens with no visible code at the call site, so a failure would be a surprise nobody can see coming

Nothing at the call site shows that a conversion runs. If it can fail or lose information, make it `explicit` so the caller has to write a cast.

cards.q: What does public char this[int x, int y] declare?
cards.a:
an indexer used as grid[x, y]

An indexer is a property with parameters, reached with square brackets.

cards.q: Which collection hands out the item with the smallest priority next?
cards.a:
`PriorityQueue<TElement, TPriority>`

`PriorityQueue` dequeues the element with the lowest priority first. `Queue` is first in, first out, and `Stack` is last in, first out.

cards.q: What is the difference between a read-only view and an immutable collection?
cards.a:
A read-only view only blocks changes through that reference; an immutable collection can never change

A `ReadOnlyCollection` wraps a list that its owner can still change, and the view shows those changes. An immutable collection has no way to change at all.

cards.q: You need to iterate keys in sorted order while adding and removing often. Which fits?
cards.a:
SortedDictionary<K, V>

A SortedDictionary keeps its keys in order after every change, at O(log n) per operation.

cards.q: Does an attribute do anything on its own?
cards.a:
No: it is data that some code must read and act on

An attribute is only metadata stored with the code. It has an effect only when the compiler, a framework or reflection code looks for it.

cards.q: Why prefer `nameof(Counter.Add)` to `"Add"` in reflection code?
cards.a:
The compiler checks `nameof`, so a rename updates it or causes a compile error

`nameof` becomes the same constant string at compile time, so it is not faster. The gain is that a typo or rename is caught by the compiler instead of failing at run time.

cards.q: Which call creates an object of a Type t without naming its class in code?
cards.a:
Activator.CreateInstance(t)

Activator.CreateInstance calls the type's parameterless constructor at run time.

cards.q: Does `numbers.AsSpan(1, 4)` copy the elements?
cards.a:
No: it is a view over the same array

A span is a pointer and a length over existing memory. Nothing is copied, so `span[0] = 9` changes `numbers[1]`.

cards.q: Why can a `Span<T>` not be a field of a class?
cards.a:
It may point into a stack frame that the object outlives

`Span<T>` is a `ref struct`, allowed only on the stack, so it can never dangle. Store a `Memory<T>` in a field instead.

cards.q: Which avoids creating new strings while splitting "a,b,c"?
cards.a:
slicing line.AsSpan() at each comma

Spans view the original characters; Split and Substring create new strings.

cards.q: Why write regex patterns as `@"..."` strings?
cards.a:
A backslash stays a backslash, so `\d` needs no doubling

Regex patterns are full of backslashes. In a normal string `\d` would have to be written `\\d`; `@"..."` keeps them as written. It changes nothing about how the regex runs.

cards.q: Why is `ToUpper()` without a culture risky for identifiers?
cards.a:
It uses the current culture, and some (Turkish, for example) change letters differently

In Turkish, `"i".ToUpper()` gives "İ", so the same code gives different results on different computers. Use `ToUpperInvariant()` or an ordinal comparison.

cards.q: Which is right for comparing two file extensions ignoring case?
cards.a:
StringComparison.OrdinalIgnoreCase

Extensions are identifiers, not text for people: compare them ordinally, ignoring case.

cards.q: When is an `IAsyncEnumerable<T>` better than a `Task<List<T>>`?
cards.a:
When results arrive over time and can be handled one by one

With `await foreach`, the consumer can start on the first item as soon as it arrives. A `Task<List<T>>` makes the caller wait until every item is ready.

cards.q: What does a bounded channel do when it is full and its mode is `Wait`?
cards.a:
The writer's `WriteAsync` waits until a reader makes room

Waiting is back-pressure: a fast writer is slowed to the reader's pace. Dropping items is what the `DropNewest`, `DropOldest` and `DropWrite` modes do.

cards.q: How does a consumer's await foreach over channel.Reader.ReadAllAsync() know to stop?
cards.a:
When the writer calls Complete() and the channel is empty

`Complete()` marks the end of the data; `ReadAllAsync` finishes once the remaining items are read.

cards.q: What is the difference between `Join` and `GroupJoin`?
cards.a:
`Join` drops items with no match; `GroupJoin` keeps them

`Join` gives one result per matching pair, an inner join. `GroupJoin` gives one result per item of the first sequence with all its matches, possibly none.

cards.q: Why might a LINQ query run more slowly than expected inside a loop?
cards.a:
Deferred queries run again every time they are enumerated; `ToList()` runs them once

A query is a recipe, not a result. Enumerating it inside a loop repeats all the work each time unless the results are stored.

cards.q: numbers.Where(n => n > 2) is assigned to q, then 5 is added to numbers. What does q.Count() count?
cards.a:
every number above 2, including the 5

The query is deferred, so it runs when Count is called and sees the current list.

cards.q: What does `[_, .., 0]` match?
cards.a:
A list of at least two elements whose last element is 0

`_` needs one element, `..` matches zero or more, and `0` must be the last element. So the shortest match is two elements.

cards.q: Why is `{ }` a useful pattern?
cards.a:
It matches any value that is not null

An empty property pattern has no conditions except that the value is not null, so `if (x is { } value)` checks for null and names the value. `var` is the pattern that also matches null.

cards.q: Which pattern matches a char that is a letter from a to z?
cards.a:
>= 'a' and <= 'z'

Relational patterns combined with and express a range.

cards.q: Why could `T total = 0;` not work in a generic method before C# 11?
cards.a:
T could not be required to have a zero or a `+` operator

T might not be a number, and constraints could only require instance members. C# 11's static abstract members let `INumber<T>` require `T.Zero` and `+`.
cards.lessonTitle: Generic Math and Static Abstract Members

cards.q: What is the difference between `CreateChecked` and `CreateSaturating`?
cards.a:
CreateChecked throws on overflow; CreateSaturating clamps

`byte.CreateChecked(300)` throws an OverflowException and `byte.CreateSaturating(300)` gives 255, the maximum. Wrapping around is what `CreateTruncating` does.
cards.lessonTitle: Generic Math and Static Abstract Members

cards.q: Which constraint allows a generic method to use T.Parse(text, provider)?
cards.a:
where T : IParsable<T>

IParsable<T> declares a static abstract Parse method that every implementing type provides.
cards.lessonTitle: Generic Math and Static Abstract Members

cards.q: Why store moments in UTC?
cards.a:
UTC has no daylight saving jumps and is the same everywhere

Local times repeat or skip an hour at daylight saving changes and differ between places, so UTC values compare and sort correctly. Convert to local time only to display.

cards.q: Which culture should a CSV file your program writes and reads use for numbers?
cards.a:
`CultureInfo.InvariantCulture`, so the file reads back the same on any computer

With the current culture a German computer writes 1,5, which breaks the commas of a CSV and reads back differently elsewhere. The invariant culture is fixed.

cards.q: A TimeSpan of 200 minutes: what are Hours and TotalHours?
cards.a:
3 and 3.33

Hours is the whole hours part; TotalHours is the full length expressed in hours.

cards.q: Why is `IEnumerable<Cat>` usable as `IEnumerable<Animal>` but `List<Cat>` is not usable as `List<Animal>`?
cards.a:
`IEnumerable<out T>` only gives items out; `List<T>` also takes items in, so it must stay invariant

If a `List<Cat>` were a `List<Animal>`, you could add a dog to it. A sequence you can only read from has no such risk, so it is covariant; no copy is made.

cards.q: How many copies of a static field in `Box<T>` exist after using `Box<int>` and `Box<string>`?
cards.a:
Two: each closed generic type has its own static fields

`Box<int>` and `Box<string>` are different types at run time, and each has its own copy of the static field.

cards.q: Which assignment compiles?
cards.a:
IEnumerable<object> e = new List<string>();

IEnumerable is covariant for reference types. List is invariant, and variance does not apply to int.
